articles.label: ACCOUNTABILITY
articles.headline: Escambia County's $47 Million Reserve Fund Sits Untouched While Roads Crumble
articles.dek: The county commission has spent three budget cycles debating infrastructure priorities. Meanwhile, the rainy day fund grows and Scenic Highway potholes multiply.
brief: Escambia County's general fund reserve has grown to $47.2 million, exceeding the commission's own 20% target by nearly $12 million
Road maintenance requests have been deferred for three consecutive budget cycles while commissioners debate a comprehensive infrastructure plan
Scenic Highway alone has accumulated 47 documented potholes since January, with some sections showing base layer deterioration
articles.body:
The pothole on Scenic Highway near the 12th Avenue intersection has been there since February. It started as a crack. Then a divot. Now it spans nearly two feet across, deep enough that motorcyclists swerve into the oncoming lane to avoid it.

Gary Hutchins drives past it twice a day on his way to work at the port. He's watched it grow.

"I called 311 in March," Hutchins said. "They told me it was on the list. Still waiting."

Fourteen miles away, in the county administrative complex on Palafox Street, a different number sits on a spreadsheet: $47.2 million. That's the current balance of Escambia County's general fund reserve, according to documents presented at the April 18 commission meeting. The figure represents 23.6% of the county's operating budget—well above the 20% target commissioners established in 2019.

The excess amounts to roughly $11.8 million.

Three Years of Deferrals

The county's Public Works Department has submitted infrastructure funding requests in each of the last three budget cycles. Each time, commissioners have deferred action, citing the need for a comprehensive infrastructure priority plan.

That plan does not yet exist.

"We've been working on developing a systematic approach to infrastructure investment," District 3 Commissioner Lumon May said during the April meeting. "We want to make sure we're spending taxpayer dollars wisely and not just reacting to squeaky wheels."

The squeaky wheels, in this case, include 47 documented potholes on Scenic Highway alone since January 1, according to 311 service request data obtained by The Flightline. Bergman Road in Cantonment has 23. Saufley Field Road shows 31.

Public Works Director Tom Curry declined to comment for this story, referring questions to the county administrator's office. County Administrator Wes Moreno did not respond to three requests for comment submitted over two weeks.

The Reserve Policy

Escambia County's reserve fund policy, adopted in 2019, establishes a target of maintaining between 15% and 20% of the general fund operating budget in reserve. The stated purpose: protecting against economic downturns, natural disasters and unexpected revenue shortfalls.

The policy does not prohibit the commission from spending reserves above the 20% ceiling. It simply doesn't address the scenario.

Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, who represents District 1, raised the reserve balance during budget discussions last October.

"At what point does fiscal responsibility become fiscal paralysis?" Bergosh asked, according to meeting minutes. "We have roads deteriorating faster than we're fixing them, and we're sitting on money we don't need to sit on."

No vote was taken. The discussion moved to other agenda items.

The Cost of Waiting

Road maintenance follows a predictable pattern, according to civil engineering studies. A crack becomes a pothole. A pothole becomes a patch. Enough patches, and the road needs resurfacing. Wait long enough, and the base layer fails. Then you're looking at full reconstruction.

The cost difference is substantial. The Florida Department of Transportation estimates routine maintenance at roughly $3,000 per lane mile annually. Resurfacing runs $100,000 to $200,000 per lane mile. Full reconstruction can exceed $1 million.

Scenic Highway runs approximately 8.2 miles within unincorporated Escambia County jurisdiction. Much of it was last resurfaced in 2014.

Jim Henderson has lived on Scenic Highway for 22 years. He's watched the road cycle through good and bad conditions. This, he says, is the worst he's seen.

"The section in front of my house, you can see the old bricks showing through," Henderson said, referring to the historic brick pavement that underlies parts of the road. "That's not a pothole problem. That's a road-is-failing problem."

What's Next

The commission is scheduled to begin FY 2027 budget workshops in June. Infrastructure funding is listed as a discussion item on the preliminary agenda, according to documents posted on the county website.

Whether that discussion produces action remains to be seen. The comprehensive infrastructure plan that commissioners have referenced since 2023 has no public timeline for completion. No consultant has been hired. No scope of work has been published.

The reserve fund, meanwhile, continues to collect interest. At current rates, it will add approximately $1.9 million by the end of the fiscal year.

The pothole on Scenic Highway continues to collect rainwater.

Gary Hutchins still swerves around it every morning.

"Someone's going to blow a tire or worse," he said. "And the county will say they didn't have the money to fix it."

articles.label: DEVELOPMENT
articles.headline: The Last Fish House on Bayou Texar Is Surrounded by Condos. Its Owner Isn't Selling.
articles.dek: Bobby Hernandez has operated his bait shop since 1987. The developers offering seven figures don't understand why he keeps saying no.
brief: Bobby Hernandez's bait and tackle shop sits on one of the last undeveloped parcels on Bayou Texar's east shore, surrounded by luxury condominiums built over the past decade.
At least four development groups have made offers exceeding $1 million for the property since 2019, according to Escambia County property records and interviews.
Hernandez, 71, says he has no succession plan and no intention of selling while he's still breathing.
articles.body:
The live shrimp tank at Hernandez Bait & Tackle needs a new aerator. Bobby Hernandez knows this because he can hear it struggling from his folding chair on the dock, a metallic wheeze cutting through the 6 a.m. quiet of Bayou Texar. He's known for three weeks. Parts are on order from a supplier in Mobile.

"They don't make 'em like they used to," he says, not looking up from the cast net he's mending. "The tanks or the suppliers."

Behind him, a seven-story condominium called The Bayou Grande throws its long morning shadow across his property line. To the north, another luxury development, Texar Pointe, gleams white against the water. His fish house—a 1,200-square-foot wooden structure with a hand-painted sign and a live well built into the dock—sits between them like a brown tooth in an otherwise perfect smile.

Hernandez, 71, has operated this bait shop since 1987. He bought it from the widow of a commercial fisherman who'd worked these waters since before the Bayou Texar bridge existed. The current assessed value of his 0.4-acre parcel, according to Escambia County Property Appraiser records, is $89,000. The offers he's received tell a different story.

"Last one was one-point-two," he says. "Million, I mean. From some group out of Birmingham."

He said no.

'They don't get it'

The transformation of Bayou Texar's eastern shore from working waterfront to luxury residential began in earnest around 2008, when the first of the current crop of condominiums broke ground on the site of a former marine repair yard. Since then, according to a Flightline review of Escambia County building permits and property transfers, fourteen residential developments have been completed within a half-mile of Hernandez's property.

The median sale price for condominiums in these developments exceeded $425,000 in 2025, per Escambia County Clerk of Court records. Several penthouses at Texar Pointe sold for more than $800,000.

Hernandez's bait shop, with its irregular hours, working dock, and parking lot that turns to mud after heavy rain, does not fit the aesthetic. The homeowners association at The Bayou Grande has twice sent letters to Escambia County Code Enforcement regarding his property—once about his exterior signage, once about a derelict boat that sat in his lot for several months in 2023.

Both complaints were dismissed. The sign predates current code. The boat, Hernandez says, belonged to a customer who died, and he was waiting for the family to claim it.

"They want me gone," Hernandez says of his condominium neighbors. "They don't say it like that. They say they want to 'discuss the future of the waterfront.' But I know what it means."

He's attended two meetings organized by residents of the adjacent developments to discuss "bayou beautification." Both times, he says, the conversation turned to his property within minutes.

"One lady asked if I'd considered retiring," he recalls. "I told her I'd consider it when I'm dead."

The offers

Since 2019, at least four development groups have made formal offers for Hernandez's property, according to documents he shared with The Flightline and corresponding records in the Escambia County Clerk's office.

The first, in 2019, came from a Pensacola-based LLC called Texar Development Partners. They offered $650,000. Hernandez declined in writing.

In 2021, a group affiliated with the developers of The Bayou Grande offered $875,000, with an additional provision allowing Hernandez to lease back a small portion of the dock for five years. He declined.

The 2024 offer from the Birmingham group—Yellowhammer Coastal Properties LLC, according to Florida Division of Corporations records—was the highest at $1.2 million. Their proposal included relocation assistance and a $50,000 "transition bonus."

Hernandez's response, according to a copy of the letter he provided: "No thank you. Not interested. Please don't contact me again."

A representative for Yellowhammer Coastal Properties did not respond to a request for comment.

'This is what I do'

On a Tuesday morning in late April, three customers came to Hernandez Bait & Tackle before 8 a.m. One bought a bucket of live shrimp. One bought a fishing license—Hernandez is one of the few remaining retailers in Escambia County authorized to sell them. One, a man in his seventies who arrived in a truck older than the building, came only to drink coffee and complain about the Pensacola Blue Wahoos' pitching.

"That's Eugene," Hernandez says after the man leaves. "He's been coming here since before I bought the place. He doesn't fish anymore. Bad shoulder. He just comes to sit."

This, Hernandez says, is what the developers don't understand.

"They see a piece of land. They see water access and a view and what they could build here," he says. "They don't see Eugene. They don't see the kids who come here to learn to throw a cast net. They don't see the guys from NAS Pensacola who come here on their day off because it reminds them of home."

He doesn't have children. His wife, Maria, died in 2018. He has a nephew in Tampa who visits once a year and has expressed no interest in the bait business.

Asked what happens to the property when he's gone, Hernandez shrugs.

"Maybe the state buys it. Makes it a park or something," he says. "Maybe the condo people finally get what they want. I won't be here to see it."

He returns to mending his cast net. The aerator wheezes. Across the water, someone on a Texar Pointe balcony is doing yoga.

"People ask me why I don't take the money," Hernandez says after a long silence. "One-point-two million. I could go anywhere. Do anything." He looks out at the bayou, where a brown pelican has just surfaced with a mullet in its bill. "But this is where I am. This is what I do. What else is there?"

The Escambia County Property Appraiser's office confirmed that no sale or transfer of the property is currently pending. Hernandez's business license with the Florida Department of Agriculture remains active through 2027.

The aerator parts, he says, should arrive next week.

articles.headline: Blue Angels Homecoming Week Brings $31 Million to Pensacola. Most of It Never Leaves the Beach.
articles.dek: Downtown merchants say the annual air show crowds skip the historic district entirely. A new shuttle proposal aims to change that.
brief: Visit Pensacola estimates Blue Angels Homecoming 2025 generated $31.2 million in direct spending, but downtown merchants report flat or declining sales during the event.
GPS data from event organizers shows 87% of air show attendees never crossed the Three Mile Bridge into mainland Pensacola.
Escambia County commissioners will hear a proposal next month for a free shuttle connecting Pensacola Beach to the downtown historic district during major events.
articles.body:
The parking lot at Peg Leg Pete's was full by 9 a.m. on the Saturday of Homecoming week. Down the road at Casino Beach, families had staked out blanket territory since dawn. The line at Crabs We Got 'Em stretched past the t-shirt shops and around the corner.

Eleven miles west, on Palafox Street, Sarah Chen watched a single customer walk through the door of her gift shop all morning.

"I used to close for Homecoming," Chen said. "Now I stay open because I keep hoping. But the numbers don't lie. This is one of our slowest weeks of the year."

The Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show, held each November at Naval Air Station Pensacola, draws an estimated 150,000 spectators over two days. Visit Pensacola, the county's tourism marketing organization, pegged the 2025 event's economic impact at $31.2 million in direct visitor spending—hotel rooms, restaurant meals, rental cars, beach chairs.

But a new analysis of that spending reveals a geographic pattern that has downtown business owners questioning whether the rising tide lifts all boats, or just the ones anchored on Santa Rosa Island.

The data gap

Visit Pensacola's $31.2 million figure comes from a methodology that estimates spending based on hotel occupancy rates, average daily rates, and visitor surveys conducted at the air show. The organization does not track where within the county that money lands.

"We measure destination-level impact," said Marcus Webb, Visit Pensacola's director of research. "We're not in the business of picking winners and losers between neighborhoods."

But GPS mobility data tells a more specific story.

EventTrack Analytics, a firm contracted by Homecoming organizers to measure crowd flow and parking utilization, provided aggregated data to The Flightline showing that 87% of devices that pinged at the NAS Pensacola air show site also pinged on Pensacola Beach during the event weekend. Only 23% showed any activity in the downtown Pensacola census tract.

That 23% includes people who live downtown, commute through it, or stopped for gas on the way to the interstate.

"The air show happens on the base. The base is surrounded by beach hotels. People watch the show, go back to their hotel, eat at the beach, and leave Sunday morning," said Tom Brennan, who has owned a restaurant on South Palafox for 22 years. "Downtown isn't on the way to anything for these folks."

A tale of two weekends

Brennan pulled his sales records for the past five years of Homecoming weekends. His revenue has declined an average of 12% compared to the same weekend in non-Homecoming years.

"People who live here assume everything's packed. They stay home," he said. "So we lose our regulars and don't gain anyone new."

The pattern holds across the downtown business improvement district. A survey of 34 Palafox-area merchants conducted by the Downtown Improvement Board in December found that 26 reported flat or declining sales during Homecoming 2025 compared to 2024. Only three reported increases, and those were bars that stay open past midnight.

Meanwhile, Pensacola Beach businesses describe the opposite problem: too much demand, not enough capacity.

"We turn people away," said Maria Santos, general manager of a Via de Luna seafood restaurant. "Friday and Saturday of Homecoming, we're on a two-hour wait by 5 p.m. The kitchen can only do what it can do."

Portofino Island Resort reported 100% occupancy for Homecoming week at rates 40% above their November average. The Hampton Inn on Pensacola Beach was sold out by August.

The economic activity is real. It's just concentrated.

The shuttle proposal

Escambia County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh said he's heard the complaints from downtown business owners for years. Now he's proposing to do something about it.

On June 4, the county commission will hear a proposal for a free shuttle service connecting Pensacola Beach to downtown during major events—Homecoming, the Crawfish Festival, New Year's Eve, and Fourth of July.

The proposal calls for 15-passenger shuttles running every 20 minutes from Casino Beach to a downtown hub at Jefferson and Palafox. The estimated cost is $45,000 per event weekend, funded through the tourist development tax.

"We're spending TDC money to bring people here," Bergosh said. "Seems reasonable to spend a little more helping them see the whole destination, not just the beach."

The proposal has support from the Downtown Improvement Board and the Pensacola Bay Area Chamber of Commerce. Visit Pensacola has not taken a position.

Some beach business owners are skeptical.

"If people wanted to go downtown, they'd go downtown," said one Via de Luna restaurant owner who asked not to be named because she serves on a tourism advisory board. "The shuttles will run empty and we'll have spent $45,000 to prove a point."

What the numbers don't measure

The debate over Homecoming's economic distribution reflects a larger tension in Pensacola's tourism strategy.

The beach and the historic downtown are marketed as a single destination—"Pensacola: The Westernmost City on Florida's Emerald Coast"—but function as largely separate economies with different visitor bases, different price points, and different infrastructure needs.

Downtown's recent renaissance, fueled by restaurants, boutique hotels, and a growing residential population, has been driven primarily by regional visitors and locals, not out-of-state tourists. The beach, meanwhile, depends heavily on the drive market from Alabama, Mississippi, and Louisiana—families looking for a week at the Gulf, not a walkable urban experience.

Homecoming draws both audiences but funnels them through a geographic chokepoint: the Three Mile Bridge, which becomes a 45-minute crawl on air show days.

"The bridge is the problem," said Chen, the gift shop owner. "You ask someone sitting in beach traffic if they want to drive back over for dinner downtown? They laugh."

The shuttle proposal attempts to solve that friction. Whether 150,000 air show visitors actually want a trolley ride to look at historic architecture remains an open question.

Chen isn't optimistic.

"They come to see jets," she said. "They don't come to see us."

The Escambia County Commission meets June 4 at 5:30 p.m. in the Ernie Lee Magaha Government Building. The shuttle proposal is item 14 on the published agenda.
